source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats
finding: Frame: the mind is not Bayesian-blind; the standard probability format hides the Bayesian algorithm. The same problem in natural frequencies makes the computation short and people use it. Natural sampling means counting cases as they come, with the marginal counts not fixed.
numbers: Posterior in the classic mammography problem is .078 from p(H)=.01, p(D|H)=.80, p(D|-H)=.096.
quote: One would be unable to detect a Bayesian algorithm within a system by feeding it information in a representation that does not match
limits: Evolutionary story (natural sampling) is an argument, not shown directly. The format effect is the tested part.
agent_relevance: The agent should convert any probability evidence into counts of cases (out of 1,000) before it reasons. Cheap, code-checkable step.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats - background cited by the paper
finding: Baseline failure in the standard format: physicians given the mammography problem mostly answer far too high. Eddy (1982) reported 95 of 100 physicians put p(cancer|positive) at 70-80% instead of 7.8%. Casscells et al (1978) found the same at Harvard Medical School.
numbers: Eddy 1982: 95/100 physicians estimated 70-80%; correct 7.8%.
limits: Figures are quoted second-hand from Gigerenzer and Hoffrage, who read Eddy. Original Eddy and Casscells not opened.
agent_relevance: This is the base-rate neglect target. Test our agent on this exact problem as a calibration check.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats - Study 1
finding: Study 1: 60 students solved 15 problems (30 tasks each), in probability or frequency format, with a standard or short menu of information. Frequency formats raised the share of answers that used a Bayesian algorithm, judged by both written process and result.
numbers: N=60 students (21 men, 39 women, 10 disciplines). Bayesian algorithms: standard probability 16%, short probability 28%, standard frequency 46%, short frequency 50%. Stable across 15 problems. Total answers 1,774 of 1,800.
limits: Students, not lawyers or doctors. Lab word problems. Even in the best condition half of answers were not Bayesian.
agent_relevance: Frequency format roughly triples Bayesian solutions for humans. For an LLM we only know the direction from the LLM lines. Test it, do not assume it.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats - Study 2
finding: Study 2 (run before Study 1) tested a third menu (hybrid) and relative frequencies. Relative frequency format did NOT help: it gave the same small share of Bayesian algorithms as probability format (60 vs 66 Bayesian algorithms). Only the menu, which sets how many steps are needed, mattered.
numbers: N=15 students, 24 problems each (360 maximum). Cognitive algorithm found in 67% of 1,080 judgments. Bayesian count: relative frequency 60, probability 66.
limits: Small N. Shows that 'frequency' alone is not the cause; the helpful form is absolute counts from natural sampling.
agent_relevance: Be precise: use 'out of N' counts, not '20%'. Relative-frequency wording does not help.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats - consistency and practice
finding: With frequencies participants became more consistent in the algorithm they used across problems; with probabilities they did not improve.
numbers: Consistency c: standard frequency .32 (session 1) to .49 (session 2); short frequency .61 to .76; standard probability .22 to .24 (Study 1); Study 2 standard probability .15 to .16.
limits: Consistency is a process measure from written notes.
agent_relevance: A frequency-first scaffold may stabilise the agent's procedure across items, not only its accuracy.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats - strategy shortcuts
finding: Non-Bayesian strategies were common: joint occurrence p(H&D), a Fisherian likelihood answer, and a comparison shortcut that is valid only when one error count is small. Joint occurrence was used more when p(D) was larger, a weak Bayesian intuition.
numbers: Correlation of p(D) with joint-occurrence use: .36 (Study 1, 15 problems), .47 (Study 2, 24 problems).
limits: Correlations over problems, not people.
agent_relevance: Name the common wrong shortcuts (answer the sensitivity, answer the joint). A checker can compare the final number with each wrong shortcut and flag a match.

source: Hoffrage, Lindsey, Hertwig & Gigerenzer (2000) Communicating statistical information
finding: Short Science report. Medical students and physicians do better with natural frequencies. The same paper tests legal professionals and law students on DNA evidence in rape cases.
numbers: Law: professionals and 127 advanced law students judged two rape cases with a DNA match. Evidence: profile frequency 1 in 1,000,000, sensitivity assumed 100%, false-positive rate 0.003. Correct source inference in probability format: 13% of professionals, under 1% of students. In natural-frequency format: 68% and 44%.
limits: PDF text is garbled; read from the layout column. Number of professionals not recovered. Short report.
agent_relevance: Direct legal result. Evidence format changed whether trained legal people could compute the chance the defendant is the source.

source: Hoffrage, Lindsey, Hertwig & Gigerenzer (2000) Communicating statistical information - verdict effect
finding: Format changed verdicts, not only inference. With probabilities more people voted guilty than with natural frequencies.
numbers: Guilty verdicts with probabilities: 45% of professionals, 55% of students. With natural frequencies: 32% and 33%.
limits: Two scenarios with little other evidence. No long-trial test.
agent_relevance: Presentation alone moved a decision by 13 to 22 points. An agent that reads evidence reports should normalise the format first.

source: Hoffrage, Lindsey, Hertwig & Gigerenzer (2000) Communicating statistical information - physician and HIV counselling
finding: Experts overstate predictive value. On the Casscells problem the most frequent estimate was 95% (27 of 60) and the correct one 2%. In an HIV-counselling probe, counsellors often told a low-risk client that a positive test meant near certain infection.
numbers: 27 of 60 participants gave 95%; correct 2%. HIV test: false-positive about 0.01%, sensitivity 99.9%; counsellors' answers of 99.9% or 100% versus an actual value near 50% (authors' estimate).
limits: Counsellor sample details sit in a reference (Gigerenzer et al 1998), not opened.
agent_relevance: Expert status does not protect against the transposed conditional. Do not trust the agent's own fluent confidence here.

source: Fenton, Neil & Berger (2016) Bayes and the Law
finding: Review of why Bayes is rarely used in courts and why Bayesian networks (BNs) could fix it. Core claim: lawyers and experts keep making the same errors (the prosecutor's fallacy, wrong hypothesis pairs, the 'prior misconception' that a likelihood ratio needs no prior). BNs do the calculation so a human need not.
numbers: Cases named: R v Sally Clark, R v Barry George, Lucia de Berk, People v Puckett, Collins, OJ Simpson, Sacco and Vanzetti. Covers 40 years of statistics in law.
limits: Authors advocate BNs. The paper's own measure of minimal impact is the 350-page NRC forensic report, which has little Bayes in it.
agent_relevance: Gives the standard catalogue of evidence errors our agent should self-check. The BN route fits our rule that code does the arithmetic and the model fills slots.

source: Fenton, Neil & Berger (2016) Bayes and the Law - the island example
finding: Worked example of the prosecutor's fallacy. A crime on an island of 10,000 people leaves a DNA trace. The random match probability is 1 in 1,000. The defendant matches. Wrong reading: 99.9% guilty. Right reading with the prior of 1 in 10,000: about 9%.
numbers: Prior 1/10,000, random match probability 1/1,000 (likelihood ratio 1,000). Posterior that defendant is source 9%; not-source moves from 99.99% to 91%.
limits: Assumes the true source is on the island and the test never misses. Lab error is added only in the fuller BN.
agent_relevance: A ready test item for our agent. The right answer needs a stated population (prior) and a likelihood ratio: posterior odds = prior odds x LR.

source: Fenton, Neil & Berger (2016) Bayes and the Law - likelihood ratio formalism
finding: Odds form: posterior odds = likelihood ratio x prior odds. An LR of 1000 against prior odds of 9999 to 1 against still leaves about 10 to 1 favouring the defence. The LR alone is not the probability of either hypothesis.
numbers: LR 1000 with prior odds 1:9999 gives posterior odds about 1:10.
limits: LR is meaningful only if the two hypotheses are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. The authors say UK guidelines allow non-exhaustive pairs and that this may have compromised the R v Barry George appeal argument (LR=1 read as no probative value).
agent_relevance: The schema's probability step should force an explicit hypothesis pair and check it is exhaustive.

source: Fenton, Neil & Berger (2016) Bayes and the Law - Sally Clark and Lucia de Berk
finding: Two classic misuse cases. Clark: expert said 'only a 1 in 73 million chance of both children being SIDS victims', assuming independence and phrased so as to invite the prosecutor's fallacy. De Berk: a nurse linked to many deaths; a tiny P(evidence | not guilty) was treated as proof, ignoring that some nurses will meet high death rates by chance.
numbers: 1 in 73 million. Authors add that failing to choose exclusive and exhaustive hypotheses in the Bayesian critique of Clark may have exaggerated the scale of the problem (Fenton 2014).
limits: Case facts come from other papers (Forrest 2003, Hill 2005, Meester 2007), not opened.
agent_relevance: Two patterns to check: independence assumed without proof; selection effects (a case built around one person near many events).

source: Fenton, Neil & Berger (2016) Bayes and the Law - Cohen's conjunction paradox and the evidence-accuracy idiom
finding: Cohen argued probability clashes with legal proof: two witnesses, each 70% reliable, give 0.49 for the joint claim, so the plaintiff loses though each witness supports him. Dawid answered with Bayes. A BN with a witness-accuracy node reproduces his result.
numbers: Two witnesses at 70% reliability: P(A)=P(B)=0.7, product 0.49. BN priors: witness reliable 70:30, facts 50:50; if unreliable, the witness says true or false 50:50.
limits: The paradox rests on reading 70% reliability as P(fact)=0.7, which ignores the prior. Exact BN output figures are in a chart, not read.
agent_relevance: Tells the agent to model a source's reliability as a separate node, not as the probability of the claim.

source: Fenton, Neil & Berger (2016) Bayes and the Law - objections to Bayes in law
finding: Lists the standard objections (Tribe 1971 on): priors cannot be set, double counting of statistics, not all evidence is quantifiable, no number fits 'beyond reasonable doubt', complexity for juries, and a conflict with keeping an open mind. The authors say most were refuted by Edwards 1991, Koehler 1992, Berger 2014, Tillers and Gottfried 2007.
numbers: No numeric results. The UK Forensic Science Service verbal scale for LRs (Puch-Solis 2012) is criticised (Mullen 2014).
limits: Advocacy review: one side of a live debate. Not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Where the objections hold: priors are a real input choice. The agent should report posteriors over a range of priors, not one number.

source: Thompson & Schumann (1987) Interpretation of statistical evidence in criminal trials: the prosecutor's fallacy and the defense attorney's fallacy
finding: Origin of the names. Prosecutor's fallacy: treat P(evidence | innocent) as P(innocent | evidence). Defence attorney's fallacy: say a match is irrelevant because many others also match, forgetting that the match still raises the odds.
numbers: Numbers not read this session; paywalled. No figures quoted from memory.
limits: Existence and title confirmed by a Crossref search and the Fenton paper's citation list. Mock-juror data not checked.
agent_relevance: Put both fallacies on the error checklist. A fix for the prosecutor's fallacy can swing the agent into the defence fallacy.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1982) and Bar-Hillel (1980), the cab problem, as cited by Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995)
finding: The cab problem: most cabs are of one colour, a witness is 80% accurate, and people answer near the witness accuracy as if the base rate did not exist. This is the founding legal-style base-rate neglect result.
numbers: Typical answer about 80%, Bayes value 41% for the standard 85/15 version (from memory of the standard problem; originals not opened).
limits: Not opened; cited by Gigerenzer and Hoffrage as a probability-format study. Later work (Koehler 1996) argues base rates are used when causal or relevant and that the fallacy is overstated.
agent_relevance: Minimal test of witness accuracy versus base rate. The agent should state both numbers and multiply.

source: Koehler (1996) The base rate fallacy reconsidered (as cited by Li & Rui 2024)
finding: Review arguing that human base-rate neglect is not as general as early work claimed; replications of the lawyer-engineer problem show partial base-rate use. Li and Rui use it for a human comparison column.
numbers: Li and Rui's human column: base rates 70/30, normative posterior-odds ratio about 5.44, humans about 2.25 for an uncharacteristic description.
limits: Koehler was not opened; second-hand through Li and Rui, who also use Kahneman and Tversky 1973.
agent_relevance: Humans are partly Bayesian. The right benchmark for the agent is partial base-rate use, not zero.

source: Li & Rui (2024) Dual traits in probabilistic reasoning of large language models
finding: Three tests of six LLMs (gpt-4o, gpt-4, claude-3-opus, gemini-1.5-pro, mistral-large, llama-3-70b) on posterior judgment. In the lawyer-engineer 'Jason' test, with an uncharacteristic description 4 of 6 models were normative, but with a stereotype-fitting description all ignored the base rate.
numbers: Normative posterior-odds ratio (75% vs 25% prior) is 9. Uncharacteristic description: gpt-4o 9, gpt-4 9, claude-3-opus 8.86, gemini 6.36, mistral 3, llama 9, human 2.25. Representative CS description: 1.25, 1.18, 1.68, 2.58, 1.62, 1.52, human 2.02. Humanities description: 1.0 to 1.6.
limits: Six models of 2024; one prompt design. Human column assembled from published sources, not a new human sample.
agent_relevance: A strong model reasons by similarity when evidence looks typical. The agent must separate 'how typical' from 'how diagnostic' on purpose.

source: Li & Rui (2024) Dual traits in probabilistic reasoning of large language models - unstructured test
finding: When base rates must be recalled by the model, posteriors follow similarity and not the prior. Posteriors correlate negatively with priors and almost perfectly with similarity.
numbers: Prior vs posterior Spearman -0.84 to -0.90 (p<0.01 or 0.001); posterior vs similarity Pearson 0.90 to 0.98 (p<0.001). GPT-4o gave a field-A prior of 2-4% when asked alone but recalled 10-30% inside the posterior judgment.
limits: One set of three fields; diagnosticity near 1 was judged by the same models.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model recall the base rate inside a judgement. Supply it as a number or fetch it in a separate step.

source: Li & Rui (2024) Dual traits in probabilistic reasoning of large language models - prompt change
finding: Changing one word in the semi-structured prompt ('compute', 'posterior probability') forced step-by-step Bayes computing and reversed the bias. In the unstructured test, the first three of four stronger instructions left correlations unchanged; GPT-4o computed step by step only at the last, and still used inconsistent recalled priors.
numbers: Four prompt revisions; correlations 'do not vary in magnitude or direction' until the final one.
limits: Only GPT-4o in the prompt ladder. The RLHF cause is a conjecture with no direct test.
agent_relevance: Supports having code, not wording, force the Bayes steps. Wording helps only if it triggers an explicit computation.

source: Araya (2025) Do chains-of-thought of LLMs suffer from hallucinations, cognitive biases, or phobias in Bayesian reasoning?
finding: Qualitative case study of reasoning models on Bayesian word problems. Without a hint, the models did not choose natural frequencies. When prompted they used them inconsistently, sometimes only to restate '90%' and then going back to symbolic algebra. Different models reached opposite answers on the same problem.
numbers: No accuracy table. Examples include a wrong 50% answer after a 'natural frequencies' attempt, and a correct 1,000-case solution.
limits: Few items, one author, no counts. A warning, not a rate.
agent_relevance: Even a reasoning model may need the frequency format imposed by the scaffold, not requested politely.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen & van Steenkiste (2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs
finding: Models acted as flight-recommendation assistants that must update beliefs about a user over five rounds. Off-the-shelf LLMs fell well below an exact Bayesian assistant and often stopped improving after round one. Prompt tricks did not help. Fine-tuning on the Bayesian assistant's predictions raised accuracy and transferred to hotels and web shopping.
numbers: Bayesian-tuned LLMs agreed with the Bayesian assistant on about 80% of trials, more than original or oracle-tuned models. Chain-of-thought and other prompt variations gave no meaningful gain.
limits: Sequential preference learning, not legal evidence. The fix needs fine-tuning, which our project avoids.
agent_relevance: LLMs accumulate evidence poorly across rounds. A scaffold should hold the running posterior in code, not in the model's memory.

source: Scholten, Rebholz & Huetter (2024-25) Metacognitive myopia in large language models
finding: Theory paper. Names five symptoms of LLM bias; one is neglect of base rates in conditional computation: output samples are conditioned by the prompt and ignore the size of the full population. Proposes monitoring and control, such as hidden parallel reasoning, as a repair.
numbers: Conceptual. No new base-rate experiment in this text.
limits: Not an empirical result; ties to human work by Fiedler.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism for the base-rate failure: prompt-conditioned sampling. Supports giving the full population count in the slot.

source: Smit, Lagnado, Morgan & Fenton (2016) Using Bayesian networks to guide the assessment of new evidence in an appeal case
finding: Applies a BN to a real conviction based on audio evidence where later analysis found extra sounds. The BN makes propositions, dependence and assumptions explicit, and sensitivity analysis shows which missing facts matter most.
numbers: Similarity of the sounds was the most valuable item for the activity-level proposition, followed by the TV evidence. The posterior moved with assumptions, and incomplete defence evidence could weaken the defence.
limits: One case. Probabilities are assumed, not measured.
agent_relevance: Model for saying which missing fact would change the answer most (sensitivity), instead of one point number.

source: Martire et al (2025) Exploring mock juror evaluations of forensic evidence conclusion formats within a complete expert report
finding: Two online experiments: a shoeprint expert report whose conclusion was a likelihood ratio, a random-match probability, a verbal label or a categorical statement. Format did not significantly change evidence weight or verdict. This challenges the claim that LRs confuse lay readers more than categorical claims.
numbers: Exp 1 N=446, Exp 2 N=313 (MTurk, US, jury-eligible). Higher numeracy gave less weight to the flawed evidence and fewer convictions.
limits: MTurk samples; one evidence type. Thompson and Newman (2015) found verdicts sensitive to strength under random-match probability but not under LR or verbal label (as cited here).
agent_relevance: Format effects are weaker inside a complete report than on isolated lines. Test format effects in full context.

source: Algorithms on Trial (2025) Does evaluative probabilistic reporting of forensic evidence infringe the presumption of innocence?
finding: Legal argument that LR reporting does not infringe the presumption of innocence, because it speaks to evidence under two propositions, not to guilt. The criticism comes from misreading both the expert's role and the presumption.
numbers: No data; doctrinal argument focused on probabilistic genotyping.
limits: Argument paper; no experiment.
agent_relevance: Role split: the expert gives P(E|H); the fact-finder owns the prior and the decision. Match this in how the agent reports.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Sally Clark - secondary summary of R v Clark and Hill's reanalysis
finding: Meadow squared 1 in 8,543 to get 1 in 73 million. The Royal Statistical Society said there was no statistical basis. Hill's reanalysis put double SIDS at about 4.5 to 9 times as likely as double murder, so 73 million was not the chance of innocence.
numbers: 1 in 8,543 squared = 1 in 73 million; about 700,000 live births a year in Britain. Hill odds 4.5:1 to 9:1. Court of Appeal 2003 quashed the conviction.
limits: Secondary source (a wiki). Fenton 2014 says the Bayesian reply may have exaggerated the scale (see a13).
agent_relevance: The right comparison is double SIDS against double murder, both rare, not double SIDS alone.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats - what it builds on
finding: Cosmides and Tooby (in press) converted the Casscells problem piece by piece into frequencies, raising Bayesian answers in step. When the format was mixed (frequency in, single-event probability out) the effect was cut by roughly half. Christensen-Szalanski and Beach (1982) found natural-sampling means closer to Bayes, but only means were analysed.
numbers: Mixed format cuts the effect by about half (reported second-hand).
limits: Reported second-hand.
agent_relevance: The question matters as much as the data: ask for 'how many of these cases', not a single-event probability.

source: Gigerenzer & Edwards (2003) Simple tools for understanding risks: from innumeracy to insight
finding: Single-event probabilities, conditional probabilities and relative risks confuse patients and doctors. Remedy: natural frequencies and absolute risks.
numbers: Short BMJ education article; no numbers extracted by me.
limits: Medical focus.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule: ask for absolute counts, say 'out of N'.
